el: Παλαιά αθηναϊκά, Κύμη, Μέγαρα, Αίγινα και Μάνη
title: Old Athenian and Mani: the «ου» dialects that were cut apart
status: Old Athenian extinct; Maniot traces in older speakers
lead: Before 1834, when Athens became the capital, Athenians did not say **ξύλο** but **ξούλο**, and they called a woman **γιουναίκα**. The same [u] for ancient **υ** was heard in Aegina, Megara, Kymi in Euboea, in the Mani peninsula and in Tsakonian. These scattered places are the survivors of a once-continuous Greek dialect area of the south-eastern mainland. In the late Middle Ages, Albanian-speaking Arvanites settled most of Attica, Boeotia, southern Euboea and the Argolid, and the old Greek speech survived only in islands of Greek within an Arvanite countryside. Then the new capital drew Greeks from everywhere, and Old Athenian vanished within a few generations, the most dramatic case of dialect death in modern Greek history.
facts: **Old Athens**, **Aegina** and **Megara** (one group in Trudgill's classification), **Kymi** in central Euboea (a group of its own), and the **Mani** peninsula in the southern Peloponnese.
Ancient **υ** and **οι** pronounced [u], not [i]: **σούκα** for σύκα, **σου** for συ. Tsakonian shares it.
Greek-speaking enclaves left after Arvanite (Albanian-speaking) settlement in the 14th–15th centuries.
Old Athenian and the Aegina dialect died out in the 19th century, after Athens became the capital (1834). Kymi, Megara and Mani declined in the 20th.
Its dialect is partly due to Athenians who settled there after the Venetian siege of Athens in 1688.

sections.h: How one dialect became five fragments

timeline.text: A Greek dialect area with **υ** = [u] probably stretches from Attica and Euboea to the Peloponnese. Ancient **υ** was still pronounced [y] into the 10th century, so this is a conservative pronunciation, not a later change.
Frankish and Catalan dukes rule Athens, Florentines after them; the city is small.
Albanian-speaking **Arvanites** settle in large numbers in Attica, Boeotia, Megaris, southern Euboea and the Argolid. Greek survives in Athens, Kymi, Aegina, Megara and the isolated Mani.
Ottoman Athens is a small town. In 1687 the Venetians besiege it and a shell blows up the Parthenon; when they withdraw in 1688, many Athenians flee to Aegina and Salamis.

Athens becomes the capital of Greece. Officials, merchants and refugees from the Peloponnese, the islands, Epirus and Constantinople pour in. Within a generation or two, Old Athenian is replaced by a new mixed urban speech.
Kymi, Megara and Mani lose most of their speakers to emigration and schooling.

sections.after: Look at **γροθία** and **φωτία**. These are the older pronunciations; the standard **γροθιά**, **φωτιά** come from merging the two vowels into one syllable (synizesis). Trudgill notes that Kymi has softened, palatal **κ** rather than full [tʃ], one reason he puts it in a group of its own.

sections.after: These features link the Old Athenian group to the dialects of the southern Aegean, not to the Peloponnese next door. Browning admits that we cannot yet explain where they came from.

sections.after: **Δρέμω** and **δράμη** keep the root of ancient **δραμεῖν** 'to run', which survives in the standard only in learned words such as **δρόμος** and **δρομέας**.

sections.text: The Mani, the middle finger of the southern Peloponnese, was never fully controlled by Franks or Ottomans. Its clans lived in stone towers, fought vendettas, and in 1821 were among the first to rise. The Maniot dialect shares the [u] for ancient **υ** with Old Athenian and Tsakonian (**ξούλο** 'wood'), and, like Cretan, it softens **κ, γ, χ** before **ε, ι** to [tɕ, dʑ, ɕ]. Like Kythera, it avoids synizesis. Even family names tell the region: they typically end in **-έας** in Outer Mani and in **-άκος** or, more rarely, **-όγγονας** in Inner (Mesa) Mani.
notes: In 1675–76 about 700 people from Vitylo in Mani left for Corsica, settling first at Paomia and later at **Cargèse**, where Greek was spoken into the 20th century.
Maniot dialect material is scarce: there is no chapter on Mani in the Portal for the Greek Language, and most descriptions are old. Treat details with care.

culture.text: Mani is famous for its **μοιρολόγια**, improvised laments sung by women over the dead, in fifteen-syllable verse and old dialect forms. They were collected in the 19th and 20th centuries and are among the most powerful Greek folk poetry. Patrick Leigh Fermor's travel book «Mani» (1958) introduced the peninsula, its towers and its laments to readers abroad.

questions.why: Ancient **υ** became [u] in the Old Athenian group, Mani and Tsakonian.
